images.caption: This true-colour picture shows the nuclear reactor. The large body of water in the left half of the image is the north-western end of a 12-kilometre long cooling pond, and water channels run through the network of reactor-related buildings west of the pond. Reactor number four appears on the west end of a long building north-west of the right-angled L-shaped water channel. Mixing with the network of abandoned buildings, water channels, and roads, areas of green appear—a testament to the vegetation that was growing around the site some 20 years after the accident.
images.alt: This true-colour picture shows the nuclear reactor. The large body of water in the left half of the image is the north-western end of a 12-kilometre long cooling pond, and water channels run through the network of reactor-related buildings west of the pond. images.filename: Stele of Khoiniki District with mosaic, reverse side.jpg
images.caption: Reverse view. An abandoned roadside stele "Brahin District" located within the Polesie State Radioecological Reserve (PSRER). The site is part of the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone. The mosaic featuring a wheat ear, a gear, and Belarusian folk ornaments has remained preserved in its original state since the 1986 disaster. The former highway is currently closed to public traffic.
images.alt: Reverse view. An abandoned roadside stele "Brahin District" located within the Polesie State Radioecological Reserve (PSRER). The site is part of the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone. The former highway is currently closed to public traffic.

images.caption:
Security gates in a community centre in Chernobyl, Ukraine.
The gates have integrated Geiger-Müller tubes to detect radioactive contamination.

A person enters the gate sideways, placing hands on the detector panels for a few seconds. If no contamination is detected, the barrier opens and the person can step out the other side.
